Algebra I · Lesson 1.5

Exponents

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

Multiplication compresses repeated addition into one step. Exponents do the same for repeated multiplication. Every rule in this lesson comes from counting factors. The values of zero, negative, and fractional exponents come from requiring those rules to keep working.

Problem
Ten 2s multiplied together is written 210210. Multiplying them out one at a time works, but it is slow. Instead split the ten factors into two equal groups of five, compute one group, then finish with a single multiplication. What is 210210?
Show a hint
  • One group of five 2s multiplies out to a number you know well.
Show the full solution
Five 2s multiply to 3232, and the two groups give 32⋅32=102432⋅32=1024​. That is five multiplications instead of the nine you would do taking one factor at a time.
Key idea
Exponent notation. bnbn means nn factors of bb multiplied together. The bb is the base, the raised nn is the exponent, and b1b1 is just bb, a single factor. Read 210210 as 2 to the tenth. As in 1.2, an exponent applies only to the symbol before it. The grouping in the last problem traded ten factors for two blocks of five, and it works in general. That rule is the power of a power rule, later in this lesson.
Problem
The product 8⋅328⋅32 is itself a power of 2. Each factor is itself a power of 2, so the whole product must be one too. Write 8⋅328⋅32 as 2x2x and enter xx.
Show a hint
  • Count the factors of 2 in each piece before multiplying anything.
Show the full solution
88 is three factors of 2 and 3232 is five more, so the product is eight factors of 2 in one row and x=8x=8​. Counting factors beats multiplying out to 256256 and factoring back down.
Key idea
The product rule. am⋅an=am+nam⋅an=am+n. The proof is a count. amam is mm factors of aa, and anan is nn more, so writing them side by side gives m+nm+n factors in all. Exponents add because factor counts add. The rule needs a shared base, since the count only works when every factor is the same number. 23⋅5223⋅52 mixes 2s with 5s, so it combines into no single power.
Problem
Evaluate 58555558​ without ever computing 5858 or 5555. Write the top and the bottom as strings of factors, cancel the shared ones, then multiply what is left.
Show a hint
  • How many factors of 5 are left after the cancelling?
Show the full solution
The five factors of 5 on the bottom cancel five of the eight on top, leaving 5⋅5⋅5=1255⋅5⋅5=125​. Brute force gives 390625÷3125390625÷3125 and the same answer, but it throws away the structure.
Key idea
The quotient rule. aman=am−nanam​=am−n. The same count, run in reverse. Each of the nn factors on the bottom cancels a matching factor on top, and the subtraction m−nm−n counts exactly what remains. That is why the last problem never needed the giant values, since 5855=58−5=535558​=58−5=53 straight away. Like the product rule, this one requires a shared base, because only identical factors cancel.
Problem
The expression (72)3(72)3 means three factors of 7272. Written out, it is a single power of 7, so (72)3=7x(72)3=7x for some xx. Count the total number of 7s and enter xx.
Show a hint
  • Each copy of 7272 contributes two 7s to the row.
Show the full solution
Three copies of 7272, each holding two 7s, make 2⋅3=62⋅3=6 factors of 7, so x=6x=6​. Adding to get 7575 is the common slip, since the 3 counts copies rather than extra factors.
Key idea
Power of a power. (am)n=amn(am)n=amn, because nn copies of mm factors is mnmn factors, so this time the counts multiply. A second rule follows, the power of a product. (ab)n=anbn(ab)n=anbn, since 1.3 lets you regroup nn copies of abab as nn copies of aa times nn copies of bb. This rule is why the opening split worked, since 322=(25)2=25⋅2=210322=(25)2=25⋅2=210.
Problem
Walk down the powers of 3. 34=8134=81, 33=2733=27, 32=932=9, and each step down divides by 3. Keep the pattern going past 3131 to 3030. What value does the pattern force?
Show a hint
  • What is 3 divided by 3?
Show the full solution
Each step down divides by 3, so 32=932=9 drops to 31=331=3, and one more step gives 3÷33÷3. So 30=130=1​. The reflex answer of 00 never fits, since dividing 3 by 3 cannot land there.
Problem
The pattern does not stop at 1. Take two more steps down from 3030, dividing by 3 at each step, to land on 3−23−2. Enter its value as a fraction.
Show a hint
  • Each step still divides by 3, even after the values drop below 1.
Show the full solution
One step below 30=130=1 is 1331​, and one more is 1991​, so 3−2=193−2=91​​. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, not a negative number, so −9−9 is the wrong turn.
Key idea
Zero and negative exponents. For nonzero aa, a0=1a0=1 and a−n=1ana−n=an1​. These are the only values that keep the divide-by-the-base pattern intact. The quotient rule gives the same answer, since 32323232​ equals 11 by cancelling and 32−2=3032−2=30 by the rule. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, never a negative number, so 3−23−2 is 1991​ and not −9−9.
Problem
The product rule keeps working when an exponent is negative. Evaluate 2−3⋅272−3⋅27 by adding the exponents before computing anything.
Show a hint
  • Add the exponents first. Only then evaluate the single power that remains.
Show the full solution
Add the exponents, −3+7=4−3+7=4, so the product is 24=1624=16​. The long way finds 2−3=182−3=81​ and 27=12827=128 separately and then divides, landing in the same place with more work.
Problem
Suppose the power-of-a-power rule keeps working when an exponent is 1221​. Then (491/2)2=4912⋅2=491=49(491/2)2=4921​⋅2=491=49, so 491/2491/2 must be a number whose square is 4949. What positive number is it?
Show a hint
  • Which positive number, times itself, gives 4949?
Show the full solution
7⋅7=497⋅7=49, so 491/2=7491/2=7​. Both 77 and −7−7 square to 4949, and the next block explains why the notation names the positive one.
Key idea
Fractional exponents. a1/2a1/2 is defined as the nonnegative number whose square is aa, written aa​. Nonnegative is part of the definition because both 77 and −7−7 square to 4949. Notation must name exactly one number, so the convention keeps the nonnegative one. Likewise a1/na1/n is the nnth root of aa, and am/n=(a1/n)mam/n=(a1/n)m means take the root first, then the power, which keeps the numbers small. Odd roots of negatives exist, since an odd count of negative factors stays negative, but an even root of a negative is not a real number.
Problem
Evaluate 93/293/2. The exponent offers two orders, root first or cube first. Both are legal, but only one keeps every number small.
Show a hint
  • Write 3223​ as 1221​ applied first, then 33.
  • What is 91/291/2?
Show the full solution
Take the root first. 91/2=391/2=3, and 33=2733=27​. Cubing first is legal and gives the same answer, but it routes you through 93=72993=729 before the square root, while root first keeps every number small.
Fun fact
Exponent notation is young. Descartes fixed the raised-number form in La Géométrie in 1637. Before that, writers spelled powers out in words, cubus for a third power, and computations ran on for lines.

Every rule in this lesson came from counting factors. The values of a0a0, a−na−n, and a1/na1/n were then chosen to keep those rules true. Next, 1.6 returns to expressions and evaluates them at given values. Chapter 3 brings variables into the laws you just built.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Warm up with the definition. 5454 means four factors of 55 multiplied together, nothing more. Evaluate it as a single number.
Show the solution
Group the four 55s into two pairs, each worth 2525, so 54=25⋅25=62554=25⋅25=625​. Multiplying one factor at a time gets there too, just with more chances to slip.
Practice
The product 121⋅11121⋅11 is itself a power of 1111, since each of its two factors is one. Write the product as 11x11x and enter xx.
Show the solution
121=112121=112 and 11=11111=111, so the product holds 2+1=32+1=3 factors of 1111, and x=3x=3​. The slip is entering 13311331, the product itself, when the question asks for the exponent.
Practice
Evaluate 129127127129​. Cancel the shared factors before you multiply anything, and only then compute what is left.
Show the solution
The seven factors of 1212 on the bottom cancel seven of the nine on top, leaving 129−7=122=144129−7=122=144​. Writing out 129129, a ten-digit number, reaches the same answer the slow way.
Practice
(174)3(174)3 collapses to a single power of 1717. Count the total factors of 1717 it contains and enter the exponent xx in (174)3=17x(174)3=17x.
Show the solution
Each of the three copies of 174174 contributes four factors of 1717, so there are 4⋅3=124⋅3=12 in all and x=12x=12​. Adding to get 77 confuses this with the product rule, where the factors sit side by side instead of in copies.
Practice
Evaluate 140⋅142140⋅142. One of the two factors is much simpler than it looks, so pin down its value before you multiply.
Show the solution
140=1140=1, so the product is 1⋅142=1961⋅142=196​. Any nonzero base to the zero power is 11, and the reflex answer of 00 is the usual miss.
Practice
Write 5−25−2 as a fraction in lowest terms. Decide what the negative exponent actually does to the base before touching any arithmetic.
Show the solution
5−2=152=1255−2=521​=251​​. The minus in the exponent takes a reciprocal and never attaches a sign, so −25−25 and −125−251​ are both wrong turns.
Practice
Evaluate 15−4⋅15615−4⋅156. Add the exponents before computing anything, then evaluate the small power that remains.
Show the solution
Add the exponents, −4+6=2−4+6=2, so the product is 152=225152=225​. Working out 156=11390625156=11390625 and dividing by 154154 gets there too, with far more arithmetic.
Practice
Evaluate (−1)15+(−1)16(−1)15+(−1)16. Count the negative factors in each power, decide the sign each count forces, then add the two values.
Show the solution
Fifteen negative factors pair off with one left over, so (−1)15=−1(−1)15=−1. Sixteen pair off exactly, so (−1)16=1(−1)16=1. The sum is −1+1=0−1+1=0​. An even exponent erases the sign, so a negative base does not always give a negative result.
Practice
Evaluate 1691/21691/2. The exponent names the one nonnegative number whose square is 169169, so search for that number directly.
Show the solution
13⋅13=16913⋅13=169, so 1691/2=131691/2=13​. −13−13 squares to 169169 as well, but the notation names exactly one number and the convention keeps the nonnegative one.
Practice
Evaluate (−27)1/3(−27)1/3, the number whose cube is −27−27. Decide first whether such a number can even exist, then find it.
Show the solution
(−3)3=−27(−3)3=−27, so (−27)1/3=−3(−27)1/3=−3​. An odd root of a negative exists because an odd count of negative factors stays negative, while an even root of a negative names no real number.
Practice
Evaluate 2563/42563/4. Take the fourth root first and cube the result, keeping every number in the computation small along the way.
Show the solution
2561/4=42561/4=4 since 44=25644=256, and then 43=6443=64​. Cubing first is legal but sends you through 2563=167772162563=16777216 before the fourth root.
Practice
Find the number xx that makes 4x=84x=8 true. The powers of 44 you know jump right past 88, yet an xx exists. Enter it as a fraction.
Show the solution
Write both sides in base 22. 4x=22x4x=22x and 8=238=23, so 2x=32x=3 and x=32x=23​​. No whole number works here, since 41=441=4 and 42=1642=16 straddle 88.
